Why does the ferry timetable change every fortnight?
Ines Varga · Former ferry deckhand, 1998–2006
Updated 2y

Because the boat can only use the harbour when there is enough water under it, and the hours when there is enough water move by about fifty minutes every day. A fixed timetable would have the boat sitting on the mud for half of every month.

So the first and last crossings are tied to the school day and the rest drift with the tide, and a new sheet is printed every fourteen days and put up at both slipways.

The tide. Ask anyone in the shop and they will tell you the same thing.

Tamsin Oyelaran · Studied coastal logistics
1y

Everyone says the tide, and that is right, but the fortnight is the interesting part. The tides themselves repeat on a cycle of about two weeks, from springs to neaps and back again, and the operator prints one sheet per cycle so that the pattern of the times is the same from one sheet to the next. If they printed a month at a time the second half would look completely different from the first and people would assume it was a mistake.
